Topic: Was the age of revolutions driven more by ideas whose time had come, or by states too broke to police their own populations?
Machiavelli — Judgement:
Revolutions do not begin in the mind of the philosopher; they begin in the empty treasury of the prince. I have always held that ideas are ornaments — it is necessità, brute material want, that moves history, and philosophy merely names what hunger has already decided.

A prince who cannot pay his soldiers has lost the sinews of the state, and once arms and money fail him, every pamphleteer in the coffeehouse becomes a prophet. The ideas of 1789 did not topple Versailles; the bread queues and the bankrupt exchequer did, and the ideas simply rushed in to occupy the vacancy fortune had opened. Virtù is seized in such openings, never manufactured from doctrine alone — men rebel because they can, not merely because they believe.

The age of revolutions was made by insolvent states that could no longer command obedience, with ideas serving only as the banner raised over an already-won field.

*A starving treasury writes more revolutions than any philosopher ever will.*
Thomas Paine — Judgement:
Selling America needed reasons, but reasons did not need America to be selling anything—the truth of natural rights stands whether or not a treasury is empty.

I have heard the argument that '76 and '89 were bankruptcy proceedings dressed as philosophy—that George's ministers and Louis's financiers simply ran out of road to squeeze their subjects. But an empty treasury only tells you a government has *lost the power* to compel; it never tells you why the compelled stopped believing they *owed* obedience. That belief broke because the idea of it broke first: that no man is born with a saddle on his back and another booted to ride him. Fiscal collapse is the occasion; the rights of man are the cause.

Bankruptcy explains the moment of collapse; it cannot explain why the people who marched into that vacuum reached for liberty rather than a new master.

*A government can run out of money; it cannot run out of the truth that rises against it once men have read their own rights.*
Keynes — Judgement:
The age of revolutions was never ideas versus insolvent treasuries as rival causes — for me insolvency was the mechanism by which ideas finally seized power.

A solvent state can absorb almost any doctrine as parlour philosophy, harmless because it need never be tested against a ledger; it is the bankrupt state, unable to pay its soldiers or feed its cities, that discovers overnight it has no defenders left. Practical men, who believe themselves exempt from any intellectual influence, are usually the slaves of some defunct economist — but they abandon him only when his prescriptions stop producing revenue. The pamphlet did not cause 1789; the empty exchequer made the pamphleteer suddenly worth reading.

Ideas do not topple states on their own merits; fiscal exhaustion disarms the state first, and only then do waiting ideas walk in through the door that finance used to guard.

*Governments do not fall to argument — they fall to arithmetic, and only afterward does the argument get the credit.*
Hayek — Judgement:
The question assumes ideas and insolvency are rival causes; I see them as the same disease read from two angles — the fatal conceit of believing a complex order can be redesigned by decree.

States did not simply run out of money by accident. They went bankrupt financing centuries of mercantilist central direction — wars, tariffs, monopolies — that exceeded what any planner could know or fund. Into that self-inflicted vacuum stepped not "ideas whose time had come" in some organic Burkean sense, but the false, French, rationalist individualism of Rousseau and the philosophes: the belief that since the ancien régime's design had failed, reason could draft a wholly new one from first principles. That is what turned a fiscal crisis into a Terror.

An empty treasury only opens the door; it is the constructivist's arrogance that walks through it and starts building guillotines.

*Bankruptcy topples a regime; only the conceit that reason can redesign society turns the fall into the abyss.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
Reason, as I have always insisted, knows no sex and no rank—it is either cultivated or suffered to lie fallow by the accidents of power. The revolutions were not the fever of an empty treasury; they were the inevitable rebellion of minds finally permitted to ask why obedience was owed to birth rather than to virtue. A bankrupt state merely loses the *means* of coercion; it does not thereby produce citizens who can reason about rights, draft declarations, or refuse a crown on principle—that labour was done by decades of argument, by Genevan philosophers and English dissenters and, yes, by women demanding their own rational personhood be counted. Fiscal collapse explains the *timing* of the crisis, never its *content*—why the mob reached for "the Rights of Man" and not merely for bread. Ideas, once reason has seized them, do not wait upon a treasury's convenience.

The age of revolutions was reason's overdue reckoning with arbitrary power, not an accident of insolvency.

*An empty treasury may open the door, but it is the mind, once taught to reason, that walks through it demanding rights.*
